_meta.description: Fern Editorial Playbook — narrative-driven editorial rules reverse-engineered from synchronized multi-track analysis of Fern videos. Every rule answers WHY a decision is made, not just WHAT the statistics are.

core_principle: Every editorial decision must be narratively motivated. A cut happens because the story demands it. A zoom happens because the viewer needs to focus on something. Text appears because it reinforces the spoken word. Statistics are a validation check, not a creative driver.

rhythm_pattern.description: Fern alternates between long sustained holds and rapid cut bursts. This creates a breathing rhythm — slow contemplation punctuated by montage energy.

long_hold.purpose: Sustained narration over a single image. Used during character exposition, context-setting, backstory. The image is the anchor while the voice carries the story.

rapid_burst.purpose: Illustrative punctuation. Quick visual proof of what was just said. Used when citing specific events, showing evidence, or creating montage energy.

cut_rules.description: 44% of cuts align with narrative function shifts. The remaining 56% provide visual freshness within the same narrative beat.

triggers: Story shifts from one topic/person/era to another
New evidence or proof is being introduced
Emotional tone changes (context → tension, exposition → revelation)
A name is spoken for the first time (cut to their photo/document)
A location is named (cut to photo/map of that place)
A document or artifact is referenced (cut to show it)
Same narrative beat, different visual angle on the same topic
After 8-12s on a single image, cut to another image of the same subject
Source document changes (different page, different archive)
Prevent viewer fatigue during long exposition stretches

cut_rate.note: 13.2 cuts/min is an OUTCOME of narrative cuts + freshness cuts combined. Do NOT target this number directly — let it emerge from following the rules above.

motion_rules.description: Motion type and speed are determined by narrative intent, not random distribution. Zoom speed is the primary emotional signal.

when: Drawing attention to a detail (a name, a date, a signature)
Building tension — narrator is revealing something

emotional_peak.description: Aggressive push-in at reveals, shocking facts

extreme_revelation.description: Snap zoom on the most shocking evidence. Rare — 1-2 per video. Reserved for the single most damning piece of evidence.

when: Revealing scope or scale (map showing multiple locations, crime scene wide shot)
Pulling back after an intense moment — giving viewer breathing room
Establishing a new location or setting
Transitioning from detail to big picture

scale_shock.description: Wide pull-back showing extent of damage, number of victims, geographic spread

pan_right.when: Scanning/reading a document left-to-right, showing timeline progression

pan_up.when: Reading down a document/list, scrolling archival text

pan_down.when: Scrolling protest signs, reading newspaper columns

when: Image has internal motion (video clip playing)
Newspaper headline that viewer needs time to read

visual_category_rules.description: What to show is determined by what's being said. Visual categories are narrative tools.

document_photo.when: Default visual for sustained narration. FBI files, letters, memos, legal documents, personal photos, mugshots. The backbone of every segment.
document_photo.sourcing: Government archives (FBI vault, NARA), Wikimedia Commons, Internet Archive, court records

archival_footage.when: Showing real historical events being described. Protest footage, arrest footage, press conferences, crime scene footage.
archival_footage.sourcing: AP Archive, Reuters, Internet Archive, public domain news reels

news_screenshot.when: Citing a specific news event or public reaction. Headline must be readable and relevant to current narration.
news_screenshot.sourcing: Newspaper archives, screenshot from news websites

documentary_footage.when: Longer clips from documentaries or recorded interviews about the subject.
documentary_footage.sourcing: Public domain documentaries, fair use clips

reconstructed_footage.when: Dramatic visualization of described events (re-creations, B-roll that evokes the scene).
reconstructed_footage.sourcing: Stock footage matching era and setting

title_card.when: Chapter transitions and key entity introductions only. Brief — just enough to read.
title_card.style: White serif typewriter text on dark background

text_overlay_rules.description: Text on screen ALWAYS reinforces what the narrator is saying at that exact moment. Never decorative, never random.

source_citation.when: Citing a specific source. Appears in corner of document photos. Shows credibility.

person_identification.when: First time a person is named in narration. Appears on their photo or related document.

entity_label.when: Introducing an organization, program, or concept. Brief title card.

in_frame_text.when: Text naturally present in the source material. Newspaper headlines, document text, protest signs.
in_frame_text.rule: The text visible in the image must relate to what the narrator is currently saying.

quote.format: Quoted text, often as typewriter effect
quote.when: Reading the subject's own words. Text appears as narrator reads it.
quote.example: My motive for doing what I am going to do is simply personal revenge.

chapter_transition_formula.description: Fern's chapter breaks follow a precise emotional arc, not just a card slap.

sequence.name: concluding_punch
sequence.description: The last sentence before the break is a punchy, emotionally loaded line that wraps up the current thread.
sequence.example: despite his intellect, he made some pretty dumb mistakes.

sequence.name: dramatic_silence
sequence.description: Narration stops. Music continues or swells. Visual may hold on last image or fade to black.

sequence.name: music_bridge
sequence.description: Music fills the gap. May include brief credits overlay. Emotional reset — the music signals 'we're moving to something new'.
sequence.note: Fern uses 20-40s music breaks for major chapter transitions, 5-10s for minor ones

sequence.name: chapter_card
sequence.description: Title card with chapter name. White serif on dark. Brief.

sequence.name: new_hook
sequence.description: The new chapter opens with a re-hook — a fresh compelling line or image that resets audience attention. NOT a boring context-setter.
sequence.example: Transitioning to new era with an arresting quote or shocking fact

hook_formula.description: The video opens (and each chapter reopens) with a visceral hook. Fern's hook is always a primary source — the subject's own words or the most shocking evidence.

opening_hook.technique: Subject's own words displayed as typewriter text on dark background, read by narrator in ominous tone
opening_hook.example: My motive for doing what I am going to do is simply personal revenge. I do not expect to accomplish anything by it.

mid_video_rehooks.technique: Re-engagement with a new compelling fact, quote, or piece of evidence before diving into exposition
mid_video_rehooks.purpose: Prevent viewer drop-off by resetting curiosity at each major story beat

narrative_function_visual_mapping.description: What narrative function is happening determines what visual and motion to use.

establishing_context.cuts: Every 8-12s for visual freshness, same narrative beat

evidence.visual: document_photo with visible text, or news_screenshot with readable headline
evidence.motion: zoom_in (1.5-5%/s) — drawing attention to the proof
evidence.cuts: Cut TO the evidence as narrator references it
evidence.text: In-frame text must match what narrator is describing

tension_build.cuts: Faster pacing, 2-4s segments, possible rapid montage
tension_build.text: Minimal — let visuals and voice carry tension

character_intro.visual: Photo of the person being introduced
character_intro.cuts: Cut to photo when name is first spoken
character_intro.text: FULL NAME overlay on first mention

hook.visual: Primary source (document, quote card, or dramatic archival)
hook.cuts: Hold — don't cut during a hook. Let it breathe.
hook.text: Quote being read, or striking headline

revelation.visual: The evidence that reveals the truth
revelation.cuts: Cut to the reveal artifact the instant narrator delivers the line
revelation.text: The damning text, if it's a document

transition.cuts: Fade to black, hold, fade up on new chapter

document_photo.note: Backbone visual. Long holds with slow zoom.

news_screenshot.note: Just enough to read the headline.

screen_recording.note: Showing digital evidence or website content.

music.role: Continuous underscore. Louder during silence/transitions, ducked under narration.
music.swells: Music swells at chapter transitions and before dramatic pauses
music.drops: Music drops to near-silence for the most intimate/shocking revelations

when: After delivering a shocking fact — let it land
Before introducing a new character or era
At the end of a rhetorical question

sfx.usage: Minimal — 10.9% of cuts. Fern relies on music + voice, not SFX.
sfx.type: Subtle impact_thud at major reveals only

production_checklist.description: Before each segment, answer these questions. If you can't, the segment isn't ready.
per_segment: WHY this image? What in the narration demands this specific visual?
WHY cut here? Did the story shift, or has the current image been held long enough?
WHY this motion? Is the narrator revealing (zoom in), establishing (zoom out), or scanning (pan)?
WHY this zoom speed? Does the emotional intensity of this moment justify faster/slower motion?
Is there text on screen? Does it match what the narrator is saying RIGHT NOW?
If this is a chapter break, did the previous sentence land as a concluding punch?
